result.topic_en: Euler gives the infinite power series for the two particular solutions p and q, integrates them from 0 to h, and from the end conditions eliminates the constants to obtain an equation in h and m that determines the maximum height of a column that can just support itself.
result.transcription:
$\mathfrak{A} = \frac{1}{2.3.m}$; $\mathfrak{B} = \frac{3\mathfrak{A}}{4.5.6.m} = \frac{1.3}{2.3....6\,m^2}$; $\mathfrak{C} = \frac{1.3.6}{2.3...9\,m^3}$;
$\mathfrak{D} = \frac{1.3.6.9}{2.3.....12\,m^4}$; etc.

§. 28. Pro his igitur litteris $p$ et $q$, habebimus iſtas ſeries infinitas:
$p = x - \frac{x^4}{2.3.4.m} + \frac{1.4.x^7}{2.3....7.m^2} - \frac{1.4.7.x^{10}}{2.3.....10\,m^3} + \text{etc.}$
$q = -\frac{x^3}{2.3\,m} + \frac{1.3\,x^6}{2.3....6.m^2} - \frac{1.3.6.x^9}{2.3......9\,m^3} + \text{etc.}$
quibus ſeriebus inuentis erit $y = \alpha p + g q$. Statuamus $x = h$, et quia fieri debet $y = 0$, habebimus hanc primam aequationem pro ſolutione noſtri problematis: $\alpha p + g q = 0$. At vero pro valore literae $g$ eruendo, cum ſit $g h = \int y\,dx = \alpha \int p\,dx + g \int q\,dx$, his integralibus ab $x = 0$ ad $x = h$ extenſis, habebimus primo
$\int p\,dx = \frac{1}{2}x^2 - \frac{x^5}{2.3.5\,m} + \frac{1.4\,x^8}{2.3....8\,m^2} - \frac{1.4.7.x^{11}}{2.3.....11\,m^3} + \text{etc. et}$
$\int q\,dx = -\frac{x^4}{2.3.4\,m} + \frac{1.3.x^7}{2.3....7.m^2} - \frac{1.3.6.x^{10}}{2.3.....10.m^3} + \text{etc.}$
vbi ergo, poſtquam poſuerimus $x = h$, oriri debet haec aequatio: $g h = \alpha \int p\,dx + g \int q\,dx$, vnde deducimus
$g = \frac{\alpha \int p\,dx}{h - \int q\,dx}$,
qui valor in ſuperiore aequatione $\alpha p + g q = 0$ ſubſtitutus praebet
$p + \frac{q \int p\,dx}{h - \int q\,dx} = 0$,
ſiue $h p - p \int q\,dx + q \int p\,dx = 0$, quae aequatio duas tantum quantitates $h$ et $m$ inuoluit, ex qua ergo valorem ipſius $h$ eruere licebit, hicque valor ipſam illam maximam altitudinem columnae declarabit, in qua ſe tantum non ſuſtinere valebit.

Z 3 §. 29.

items.quote: quae aequatio duas tantum quantitates $h$ et $m$ inuoluit, ex qua ergo valorem ipſius $h$ eruere licebit, hicque valor ipſam illam maximam altitudinem columnae declarabit, in qua ſe tantum non ſuſtinere valebit.
items.english: This equation involves only the two quantities h and m, so the value of h can be found from it; that value will give the maximum height of the column at which it is just barely unable to support itself.
